The spread of the Thule people, the ancestors of the Inuit, from northern Alaska east across Arctic Canada to Greenland, mostly between about 1000 and 1300. Recent dating suggests the main move was fast, perhaps within a few generations after 1200.

The Thule were expert sea hunters. They hunted bowhead whales from large skin boats called umiaks, used kayaks and dog sleds, and had toggling harpoons that stayed in the animal. A warmer climate may have opened the sea routes that whales and hunters followed, and some scholars think the search for iron, such as meteorite iron in northwest Greenland, also drew them east.

As they spread, the older Dorset people, whom later Inuit stories call the Tuniit, disappeared. In Greenland the Thule met the Norse settlers, who had arrived around 985. The Norse colonies died out in the 1400s; the Inuit stayed, and their language and way of life now stretch from Alaska to Greenland.
